analysis.one_liner: Strips seven-year market exclusivity from orphan drugs that turn out to be commercially profitable within 12 years.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote: it was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee on January 24, 2023, sent to its Health Subcommittee on February 3, 2023, and died there with zero cosponsors when the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current law, a drug company can get seven years of FDA-protected market exclusivity for a drug designated as an "orphan drug" — a drug for a rare disease that the company said it could not sell profitably. Some drugs that win that designation on the grounds that sales would never cover development costs go on to earn enormous profits while keeping their monopoly protection. This bill would let the FDA keep that exclusivity only if the company could still show, looking at expected sales over the first 12 years, that the drug would not pay for itself — and it would count sales of all of the company's related drugs covered by the same orphan designation, so companies could not split a profitable drug across applications to keep each one looking unprofitable. It was introduced in January 2023, referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Health Subcommittee, and never received any further action.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients with rare diseases and everyone who pays for their care — families, insurers, and government programs like Medicare and Medicaid — would benefit if competitors could enter the market sooner for drugs that were awarded orphan exclusivity on the claim that they could never be profitable, but that turned out to earn back their development costs many times over. Generic drug makers would also gain earlier market access.

how_it_helps.text: Under current law, a drug designated as an orphan drug because it was thought too unprofitable gets seven years of FDA market exclusivity regardless of how much money it later makes; this bill conditions that exclusivity on the sponsor actually still expecting not to recover development costs within 12 years of U.S. sales.

When judging cost recovery, the FDA must count sales from all of the sponsor's related drugs covered by the same orphan designation, so a company cannot split a profitable franchise across multiple applications to keep each one looking unprofitable.
If exclusivity was granted and the drug turns out to be commercially successful, the FDA is directed to revoke the exclusive approval, opening the market to competitors sooner.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name pharmaceutical companies would lose up to seven years of monopoly market exclusivity on qualifying rare-disease drugs, and possibly some marginal research investment in rare diseases whose profit outlook sits near the line the bill draws.

drawbacks.text: The bill adds a condition to the incentive that Congress created to encourage development of drugs for rare diseases, and drugmakers and some patient groups argue that weakening exclusivity reduces the reward for taking on diseases so rare that they would otherwise never be profitable to treat.

Requiring the FDA to forecast whether a sponsor will recover development costs over the first 12 years of U.S. sales is an inherently uncertain prediction, which could produce contested decisions and litigation over each designation.

The bill applies only to orphan drugs designated under the cost-recovery criterion (drugs claiming they would not be profitable), not to the broader rare-population criterion, so the number of drugs affected is narrower than the title might suggest.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The upside is real but narrow: it targets only drugs that got orphan status by claiming they could not be profitable, then became profitable anyway, and it gives those drugs 12 years of sales to prove whether recovery actually happened. That is a reasonable test rather than a blanket cut to orphan incentives. The downside an honest supporter must acknowledge is that forecasting 12-year revenue is hard for both the FDA and drugmakers, which could deter development of genuinely risky rare-disease drugs and lead to case-by-case fights over projections. On balance the bill addresses a well-defined loophole at modest risk to the incentives that matter most.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Health Subcommittee, and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on January 24, 2023 and referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.
On February 3, 2023 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health, where the record shows no further action.
The bill attracted zero cosponsors during its two years in Congress.
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and bills not passed by both chambers die at the end of a Congress and must be reintroduced from scratch.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug makers are better off: they keep seven-year market exclusivity on orphan drugs designated as unprofitable even when those drugs turn out to be blockbusters, with no new test of whether the incentive is still warranted.

for.name: Rep. Earl L. "Buddy" Carter
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on January 24, 2023 to limit FDA market exclusivity for profitable orphan drugs.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Health Subcommittee on February 3, 2023 and took no further action on it — no hearing, no markup, no floor consideration in two years.

against.name: House Subcommittee on Health
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and never acted on the bill for the remainder of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a Republican sponsor and zero cosponsors of either party, so no partisan pattern of support or opposition ever formed; it simply died in committee without a vote.

industries.industry: Brand-name and specialty drug makers with orphan-designated products
industries.note: Companies would lose or forgo seven years of FDA market exclusivity for drugs designated as unprofitable that turn out to be commercially successful within 12 years, shortening the period during which they can charge monopoly prices. Their interest runs against patients and payers who bear those prices.
Ending exclusivity early on blockbuster drugs labeled unprofitable would let generic competitors enter the market sooner, which is how prices come down for patients and insurers.
